content: These symptoms may include a downward deviation of the eyes (commonly referred to as sunsetting eyes), irritability, and episodes of vomiting. The causes of macrocephaly can vary widely. It may be due to benign familial macrocephaly, which is a hereditary tendency for larger head sizes within a family. Other potential causes include Canavan disease, Hurler syndrome, hydrocephalus (which may be congenital, post-traumatic, or obstructive in nature), intracranial bleeding, and Morquio syndrome. Healthcare providers typically identify macrocephaly during routine well-baby examinations. During these evaluations, the provider will take a detailed medical history and perform a thorough physical examination. Questions may focus on the timing of the head size changes, such as when the head first appeared larger than expected and whether the head size is increasing disproportionately compared to the rest of the body. The provider may also inquire about the specific pattern of head growth, such as whether the enlargement is uniform or more pronounced in a front-to-back or side-to-side direction. Additionally, they will ask about any accompanying symptoms, particularly those related to brain or nervous system function. A comprehensive physical examination will also be conducted to evaluate the child’s overall growth and developmental milestones. If macrocephaly is confirmed, further diagnostic testing is often required to determine the underlying cause. Common imaging studies include a computed tomography (CT) scan of the head or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, which can provide detailed information about the structure and potential abnormalities within the skull and brain. If you suspect macrocephaly or notice unusual head growth in a child, it is essential to seek medical care promptly. Early diagnosis and intervention can help address the underlying cause and prevent potential complications.
